This is not a game. It's more like a fancy choose your own adventure book. See the  Wikipedia page if you want to know the story before hand.  

I did not enjoy this experience, i did not find it fun, and here are my main complaints:

1) You spend all of your  time sifting through emails and texts looking for important information or data chunks. This is not a challenge because the information is highlighted for you. To make matters  even dumber, the specific emails, texts, etc are marked with an icon to show you which ones have the important information you need to act on.

2) The important decision points in the game are also highlighted in bright yellow as conflicting data chunks. You have to choose which one Orwell (the computer) will consider as fact. Often times you have to do this without any way of knowing the actual truth, but the implications of the choices are always glaringly obvious. 

3) There are data chunks that have to be given to Orwell for the story to progress, even if you don't  want to provide it. This is the one thing the ruined the experience for me, and made it obvious that the program is leading you by the nose and you have no real control. I get it. You can't read a book from the middle out, and in a "game" that is basically just a click-through-story you have to proceed in the order the author intends. All the important information has to be in place for the story to make sense. 

Lastly, and this is a minor quibble, but I also take issue with the name of this "game". Orwell is a stupidly ironic name. George Orwell was an opponent of totalitarianism, not it's champion. Perhaps a better literary subject to steal would have been Colossus (Dennis Feltham Jones). At least that Colossus was a computer.

As is typical for games in this genre (like Papers Please), most of the actual game mechanics don't actually make sense as something that could actually happen in the real world, once you sit down and think about it.  But a sprinkling of suspension of disbelief later, and there's still an enjoyable game below that.

Get it if you're interested in the themes of conspiracy, espionage, and of course, Big Brother.

Most of the story is fixed puzzle solving with only really one "right" answer through each part, although there are places where you can choose one of two different answers (both of which will be accepted) in order to influence the direction of the overall story and whether specific characters get arrested or get away.  Whether this will matter to you depends on how well you can insert yourself into the story and choose sides.

Orwell is more of a story-based game, where your choice will affect the story and the ending you get at the end. The premise of Orwell is about privacy, government surveillance, and potential abuse of the access to our data.

Positives:
+ Decent story with multiple endings, enough to warrant a replay.
+ Simple but unique concept and mechanics.
* Choices matter, the effect of your choices can sometimes be seen throughout the game.

Neutral:
* Story can be too short.
* Plays more as a visual novel than actual deduction and logic puzzle..

Negatives:
- UI & UX can be a little bit annoying, though it is mostly small things.
- The game can show a little bit too much spoiler, where it will show some data doesn't match with each other even though you haven't seen or even have access to it yet.

Overall, while Orwell has some shortcomings, I would still recommend it to people who seek a story-driven game about surveillance and privacy and its effect.

This review won't matter much in the long run, but [i]Orwell[/i] just seems way over-rated to me. I'll try to explain why.

The story is needlessly convoluted, but let's set that aside.

The core gameplay mechanic (if you want to call it that) is dragging text from the right side of the screen to the left side of the screen. [b][u]That is all[/u][/b]: click to open windows to find text, then click and drag some portions of text that have been pre-selected and pre-highlighted as potentially relevant. When you drag text to the left side of the screen, it gets uploaded to the Orwell database as one of the results of your investigations. The Steam Trailer involves a bit of role-playing that doesn't quite represent gameplay accurately in this regard.

What really frustrated me was just how clumsy some of the most thematically important mechanics are. Sometimes, you find 2 "datachunks" of text (let's call them A and B) that conflict with each other, and you have to decide which one to upload. Your choice makes a difference to how the story unfolds, and affects people's lives. People can be arrested or die based on what you upload. The choices you make in situations like this constitute 100% of the moral complexity that [i]Orwell[/i] intends to confront you with. These decisions are central to the narrative, and to the player's experience.

Here's what's super lame: sometimes, when you find text A, and [i][u]before you could even possibly have an opportunity to see B[/u][/i]. the game says "A conflicts with [u]an unknown datachunk[/u]." This clumsy mechanic is in tension with the most basic plot-point of the game. The whole plot of the game is that The Nation needs [u]you[/u] to track down information and to decide what information goes into Orwell's databases. But what gameplay tells you is that [i]before you do anything[/i], Orwell already knows all the information that's out there, and knows when a conflict will arise, even when you (as the Investigator who is supposed to be influencing the story) have no idea yourself that B exists, and have done no detective work to suggest to Orwell that B exists. The whole thing is on (branching) rails, and your decisions amount to nothing more than selecting A vs. B, when Orwell can predict the conflict between A and B in advance. This means your detective work is essentially irrelevant; Orwell has done it all in advance, but won't share it with you. All that's left to matter is the choice between A and B.

One solution would've been to just let you resolve conflicts later: suppose that first you find and upload A, then later you find B, and you make a decision about whether to keep A in the database or replace it with B. But that would disrupt the game's ability to proceed with the narrative in a way that approximates a real-time unfolding of events. What the game wants to do is unfold the story as soon as you upload info to Orwell's database, irreversibly. If you upload A (whether or not you've seen B) then the A-chain of events begins. As a result, the game [b]has[/b] to tell you in advance that there's a conflict, so that you can "choose" which on-rails narrative will unfold.

So, my conclusion is that this is a game that is, fundamentally, poorly built. The core gameplay mechanics are kludges, patched together to facilitate the unfolding of the (branching) on-rails narrative. There are some choices to make, but the bulk of "investigative" gameplay is meaningless: this is a slideshow in games' clothing.
Worth it.

What was originally probably intended to be a game with an anti-surveillance message subverts that same message with its game play; if you are paying attention you can prevent a bombing, bring a murderer to justice and oust a corrupt politician. While there is a point near the end of the game where the people you are watching accuse you of ruining their lives they are, without exception, actual terrorists, a murderer, an asshole who doxxed your friend, wrong about the extent of your involvement, or some combination there of. It's easy to feel like your actions have been justified.

Message issues aside I recommend the game. It has an innovative, well executed idea and - most importantly - fun game play. It's a good game! Just don't play it looking for a coherent philosophy.
For a free game, it's quite a bit fun. And also a little bit scary if I'm honest.

The minimalist style of this game coupled with limited choices speaks volumes for one of the key messages of this game about the limitations of computers. Featuring an information retrieval software tool thrown into a largely conservative nation fraught with anti-surveillance activists creates a trilling and provocative story that puts the player into the interesting perspective of an outside investigator.

There were many points throughout this game's story where I felt I knew the right answers but the surveillance system didn't recognise those answers and there was no way for me to communicate this to my investigative partner which, while frustrating, felt intentional. The sections in which you have limited time or resources really put the crunch on me and demanded that I think quickly and effectively rather than becoming frustrated at these restrictions since there are no strict failure conditions and these moments subside to the calm and slow pace used for most of the game.

With this game the first playthrough is always the best playthrough as you experience the expert unfolding of the rich story but that's not to say there is no replay value. There are a few side plots you can influence along the way to one of the few different endings you can achieve but it mostly important to get your first playthrough good by not leaving too much time between chapters, which could break your immersion and memory of major plot points.
